## 83.3 million items per second

```
throughput = clock / II
           = 250 MHz / 3
           = 83.3 million items/s
```

The 12-cycle latency does not appear. It is paid **once**, filling the pipeline at the start; after that an item emerges every 3 cycles forever.

## Latency and II are different questions

| | Means | Matters for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Latency** | cycles from one item entering to that item leaving | response time, and how long a flush takes |
| **II** | cycles between accepting one item and the next | **throughput** |

For `n` items the total time is

```
total = latency + (n - 1) x II   cycles
```

With `n = 1,000,000`: `12 + 999,999 x 3 = 3,000,009` cycles. The latency contributes 12 of three million — four parts per million. For a long stream, **throughput is entirely II** and latency is a rounding error.

Which way round it matters flips completely for short bursts. One item takes 12 cycles whatever the II is. A ten-item burst takes `12 + 27 = 39` cycles, and halving the latency would help more than halving the II. The question "which number do I care about" is really "is my stream long or short", and getting that backwards is how people optimise the wrong figure for a week.

## Why II is 3 and not 1

A perfectly pipelined block has `II = 1` — a new item every cycle. An II above 1 means something prevents it, and there are only a few possible causes:

**A loop-carried dependency.** Iteration `i` needs a result from iteration `i-1`, and that result takes 3 cycles to compute. Nothing can start sooner than the dependency allows. This is the commonest cause and the hardest to fix, because it is a property of the algorithm rather than the implementation.

**A resource conflict.** The body needs three reads from a BRAM that has one port per cycle. The tool serialises them, and II becomes 3. Fixable: partition the array across several BRAMs, or use a dual-port configuration, and the II drops.

**A shared operator.** One DSP slice used by three multiplications in the body. Same fix — let the tool allocate three, at the cost of area.

An HLS tool reports *why* it could not reach the II you asked for, naming the dependency or the resource. That message is the most useful output of the whole flow and is routinely ignored.

## The transferable arithmetic

This is the same relationship as Little's law, and the same as a CPU's reciprocal throughput against its instruction latency. A multiply on a modern x86 core has a latency of about 4 cycles and a throughput of one per cycle: a chain of dependent multiplies runs at a quarter speed, while independent ones issue every cycle.

So the general lesson is the one worth keeping: **a dependent chain runs at the latency; independent work runs at the throughput.** Unrolling, interleaving several streams, or reassociating a reduction into a tree are all the same move — converting a dependent chain into independent work so that the throughput figure is the one that applies.

Here, if the II of 3 comes from a loop-carried dependency and you have three independent streams to process, interleaving them fills the gaps and triples the aggregate throughput without changing the hardware at all.
